study.title: Acts 26 - Paul's defense before Agrippa
study.overview: In this chapter, Paul makes his defense before King Agrippa, the governor Festus and other authorities. He not only responds to the accusations of the Jews, but also turns the moment into testimony of the gospel: his old opposition to Jesus, the experience of vision on the way of Damascus, the call to announce repentance and faith, and the affirmation that his message is in continuity with the Law and the Prophets. The chapter culminates in the public assessment that Paul deserves death or imprisonment, although he remains imprisoned for having appealed to Caesar.

outline.title: Paul gets space to defend himself
outline.explanation: Agrippa grants him permission to speak, and Paul responds with respect. He thanks for being able to defend himself before someone familiar with the customs and questions of the Jews, asking for patient attention.

outline.title: The hope of Israel and the question about the resurrection
outline.explanation: Paul recalls his life among the Jews, his Pharisaic formation and the true motive of the conflict: hope in God's promise to parents. He insists that the central question is the resurrection, something that should not seem incredible before the power of God.

outline.title: From persecution to the heavenly call
outline.explanation: Paul narrates his old hostility against the name of Jesus and the persecution of the saints, until Christ's intervention on the way to Damascus. The vision commissions him as a witness and minister to open eyes, convert from darkness to light, and proclaim forgiveness and inheritance to those sanctified by faith in Jesus.

outline.title: Obedience, preaching, rejection and final verdict
outline.explanation: Paul claims to have obeyed the vision, preaching repentance and conversion everywhere. He explains that he was persecuted for this, but insists that his message is in accord with Moses and the prophets. Festus accuses him of madness, Paul responds sobrietyly, Agrippa is confronted with the prophetic faith and the chapter ends with the public conclusion that Paul could be released, not the appeal to Caesar.

study.context: The scenario is a formal hearing in Caesarea before Roman authorities and Agrippa, who were familiar with Jewish affairs. The text shows that Paul was already imprisoned and tried because of his preaching. The notes highlight that Agrippa was a prominent figure in the assembly and that his presence made the audience especially suitable for Paul's defense.
study.theology: The chapter presents unity between the hope of Israel and the gospel of Jesus. Paul does not treat the Christian message as a rupture with the God of his parents, but as a fulfillment of the promise made to the ancestors. The resurrection occupies a central place: if God raises the dead, then the message about Jesus is not absurd, but consistent with his power. It is also clear the divine initiative in salvation: Christ appears, calls, sends and gives mission. Conversion is not only moral change; it is transfer of darkness to light, from the power of Satan to God, with forgiveness of sins and inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Jesus. The text also highlights God's sovereignty in providence: even if imprisoned, Paul remains alive and witnessing because the Lord sustains and leads his steps. Finally, the chapter counters two answers to the gospel: Festus' objection and Agrippa's hesitation, showing that truth can be recognized intellectually without complete surrendering the heart.

scholarViews.insight: Paul's defense shows that his preaching was consistent with the Jewish faith and centered on the fulfillment of the promises of the Old Testament in Jesus.
Paul received an immediate call from heaven to preach to the Gentiles; therefore his work was not rebellion, but obedience to God.
The claim that Christ should suffer confronted Jewish prejudices, which expected a only glorious and victorious Messiah.

questions: Why does Paul insist so much that his message is in continuity with Israel's hope and not against it?
What difference is there between hearing the truth with interest, how does Agrippa seem to do, and really surrender to Christ?
How can the conviction that God can raise the dead changes the way of facing suffering, persecution and injustice?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to witness with respect, clarity and courage, even in a hostile environment. It also teaches how to examine whether our faith is only in religious ideas or in real obedience to the call of Christ. In practice, it is worth responding to the gospel with concrete repentance, abandonment of sin and life consistent with the faith we profess. Moreover, when suffering seems to prevent God's work, Acts 26 recalls that the Lord can use even prisons and judgments to fulfill his purposes.
study.uncertainty: Some specific historical details about Agrippa and the audience are inferred from the notes, but not magnified beyond what was provided. Notes also differ in tone and interpretive emphasis; therefore, commentators' observations were treated as readings, not as final statements of the text. The chapter does not directly inform the later outcome of Paul's process, only records the favorable evaluation made there and the fact that his appeal to Caesar prevents immediate release.
